data.content_ref: inline:The target claims the dilemma 'dissolves' by redefining corroboration as informational content survived, not probability, and explicitly says we prefer high-content theories 'even if we assign them zero probability.' But a theory assigned zero probability is one the framework holds to be false (or at least not credibly true). Preferring theories we believe false because they are 'informative' does not dissolve the dilemma of induction—it abandons the original enterprise (rational acceptance of scientific theories for purposes of belief and action) and replaces it with a purely intellectual ranking of falsehoods-by-construction. The framework is decision-theoretically inert: if all candidate theories carry zero probability, the expected utility of any action guided by any theory is zero, so the framework cannot guide practical action at all. 'Telling us more about the world' is vacuous when the theory is assigned zero probability of being true—one cannot learn about the world from a theory one believes false merely because it rules out many possibilities. The target does not dissolve the dilemma; it changes the subject to a domain where the dilemma does not arise, leaving the original problem of rational acceptance unanswered.
